<div class="elementor-element elementor-element-199fa184 elementor-widget elementor-widget-theme-post-content" data-id="199fa184" element_type="widget" e-type="widget" widget_type="theme-post-content.default">

<div class="elementor-widget-container">

<div class="et_pb_section et_pb_section_130 et_section_regular">

<div class="et_pb_row et_pb_row_153">

<div class="et_pb_column et_pb_column_4_4 et_pb_column_155 et_pb_css_mix_blend_mode_passthrough et-last-child">

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_text et_pb_text_343 et_pb_text_align_left et_pb_bg_layout_light">

<div class="et_pb_text_inner">

**QuoIntelligence uncovers a previously unreported and undetected variant of the WIREFIRE web shell, a Python-based implant found in Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN compromised appliances.**

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_image et_pb_image_91">

<span class="et_pb_image_wrap"><img src="https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223.png" title="Breaking News- UN 5223" class="wp-image-13311" data-fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" srcset="https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223.png 2240w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-300x169.png 300w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-1024x576.png 1024w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-768x432.png 768w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-1536x864.png 1536w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-2048x1152.png 2048w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-1080x608.png 1080w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-1280x720.png 1280w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-980x551.png 980w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Breaking-News-UN-5223-480x270.png 480w" sizes="(max-width: 2240px) 100vw, 2240px" width="2240" height="1260" alt="QuoIntelligence Blog - Fake Handelsregister Invoices" /></span>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_divider et_pb_divider_164 et_pb_divider_position_center et_pb_space">

<div class="et_pb_divider_internal">

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_text et_pb_text_344 et_pb_text_align_left et_pb_bg_layout_light">

<div class="et_pb_text_inner">

## Introduction

In mid-December, security researchers from Mandiant and Volexity identified multiple web shells hidden by an unknown threat actor on internal and external-facing web applications, a global exploitation and intrusion attempt against Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliances.

The threat actor, currently tracked by Mandiant as UNC5221 and by Volexity as UTA0178, appears to be part of a Chinese state-sponsored group with advanced capabilities in network exploitation of external-facing devices. Although there is a limited degree of certainty and public reporting in their attribution, indications suggest their activities are likely driven by espionage objectives.

During these incidents, the threat actor exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-21887 and CVE-2023-46805) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure VPN to bypass authentication methods and allowing the attackers to execute malicious commands on the targeted appliances. Additional information on the exploitation chain and methodologies used can be found in Volexity’s [initial article](https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/15/ivanti-connect-secure-vpn-exploitation-goes-global/).

During our investigation, QuoIntelligence’s Research Team discovered an additional variation of a Python web shell currently tracked as WIREFIRE (by Mandiant) and <span class="ui-provider a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z ab ac ae af ag ah ai aj ak" dir="ltr">GIFTEDVISITOR</span> (by Volexity) with similar capabilities, hidden in a different file. This discrepancy is presumably attributed to the threat actor’s intent to circumvent detection mechanisms and to avoid detections by public YARA rules known.

To avoid confusion, the article will stick to the taxonomy provided by Mandiant.

At the time of reporting, public detections provided by security researchers are ineffective and will not detect this new variation, posing additional risks to compromised customers and clients that are undergoing internal investigations post-breach. The Integrity Check Tool provided by Ivanti will most likely detect a signature mismatch inside the application’s folder, however, Volexity [reported](https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/18/ivanti-connect-secure-vpn-exploitation-new-observations/) that UNC5221 was seen modifying the in-built scanner’s code to prevent reporting any mismatch and further increase the likelihood of not detecting the tampered files.

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_divider et_pb_divider_165 et_pb_divider_position_center et_pb_space">

<div class="et_pb_divider_internal">

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_text et_pb_text_345 et_pb_text_align_left et_pb_bg_layout_light">

<div class="et_pb_text_inner">

## Technical Details

During our research on Ivanti Connect Secure VPN exploits and hunts for additional samples, we identified a suspicious <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">.EGG</span> Python archive containing small variations between the original sample reported by Mandiant and Volexity.

In the original sample, WIREFIRE was located in the usual location <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">/api/resources/visits.py</span> and with the *post* function overwritten by the threat actor. However, our new finding was located inside of <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">/api/resources/category.py</span>, with the same *post* function overwritten.

The two code snippets highlighted minor differences in the methodology of data transmission and subsequent execution. POST requests with specific indicators remain the way to convey the encrypted data payload, which is then decrypted and directly executed within the memory space of the process, leaving no traces on the compromised file system.

In this particular instance, the threat actor can also rely on specifically set cookies to send the encrypted payload and will not rely on the GIF file previously seen in \`visits.py\`. If the cookie is not set, the malicious code will extract the contents of the API request containing the encrypted payload.

Our analysis highlights the emergence of a novel code addition that enables the threat actor to execute malicious code through the Python <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">exec()</span> function. This approach can facilitate the retention and persistence of data throughout successive POST requests, leveraging the <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">globals()</span> and <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">locals()</span> functions for data storage after each execution.

The following coding snippet highlights the content of the post function while redacting the value of variable *dskey*, containing a unique identifier of 16 characters used as the decryption key.

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_image et_pb_image_92">

<span class="et_pb_image_wrap"><img src="https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Picture-1.png" title="Picture 1" class="wp-image-13316" decoding="async" srcset="https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Picture-1.png 624w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Picture-1-300x134.png 300w, https://quointelligence.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Picture-1-480x214.png 480w" sizes="(max-width: 624px) 100vw, 624px" width="624" height="278" alt=": Code snippet of the function &quot;post&quot; containing the slightly modified web shell" /></span>

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_divider et_pb_divider_166 et_pb_divider_position_center et_pb_space">

<div class="et_pb_divider_internal">

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_text et_pb_text_347 et_pb_text_align_left et_pb_bg_layout_light">

<div class="et_pb_text_inner">

## Detections

When the discovery was made, the existing YARA rule from Mandiant failed to identify our latest findings, leading us to the conclusion that is it likely that threat actors are deploying new web shells in different directories and with slight modifications to evade detections and hunting by security and IT teams using the publicly available YARA rules.

The rule <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">M_Hunting_Dropper_WIREFIRE_1</span> that Mandiant provided detects the web shell WIREFIRE only if it resides inside the <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; font-weight: normal;">/api/resources/visits.py</span> due to the strings used for matching, excluding any other web shell with identical or similar code but located in different files.

To rapidly respond to this new finding, we created a less restrictive and temporary YARA rule to detect commonalities between these web shells that are in different files, achieving to identify WIREFIRE and its variations in every file inside of <span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime';">/api/resources/</span> to test its accuracy.

</div>

</div>

<div class="et_pb_module et_pb_text et_pb_text_348 et_pb_text_align_left et_pb_bg_layout_light">

<div class="et_pb_text_inner">

<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    description = “Detects the web shell WIREFIRE tracked by Mandiant and similar variants using common pack / unpack methods”</span>  
<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    date = “2024-01-19”</span>

<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">  strings:</span>

<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    \$s1 = “zlib.decompress(aes.decrypt(base64.b64decode(” ascii</span>  
<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    \$s2 = “from Cryptodome.Cipher import AES” ascii</span>  
<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    \$p1 = “aes.encrypt(t+(‘\\x00’\*(16-len(t)%16))” ascii</span>

<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">   condition:</span>

<span style="font-family: 'Courier Prime'; color: #ffffff;">    filesize \< 10KB</span>
